cards.front: What happens when an antigen enters the body and meets many different lymphocytes?
cards.back: Only the lymphocyte with a matching receptor binds the antigen and is selected. It then divides to form a clone of identical cells, a process called **clonal selection**.
cards.hint: Think about what each lymphocyte's receptor is able to recognise.

cards.front: Why can a selected B cell not respond to its antigen on its own?
cards.back: It also needs chemical signals from a **helper T cell** before it divides. Binding its antigen is only part of what it requires.
cards.hint: Think about what the B cell needs beyond its own receptor binding.

cards.front: How does a T cell receptor differ from a B cell receptor in the way it recognises antigen?
cards.back: A **B cell** receptor binds antigen directly. A **T cell** receptor binds only an antigen displayed on the surface of another cell.
cards.hint: Compare where each receptor meets the antigen.

cards.back: Clonal expansion is the repeated division of a selected lymphocyte by **mitosis**, producing many genetically identical cells.

cards.front: What are the steps a B cell goes through after its receptor binds its antigen?
cards.back: 1) It receives signals from a helper T cell. 2) It divides repeatedly by mitosis in clonal expansion. 3) Most cells differentiate into **plasma cells** that secrete antibodies. 4) Some become **memory cells**.
A **memory cell** is a long-lived lymphocyte left after an infection. It responds quickly if the same antigen returns, so the second response is faster and stronger.

cards.front: A student writes that helper T cells kill pathogens and make antibodies. What is wrong with this?
cards.back: Helper T cells do neither. They release **cytokines**, which are chemical signals that activate other cells such as B cells, cytotoxic T cells and phagocytes.
cards.hint: Look at what the helper T cell releases once it is activated.

cards.front: What are the steps by which a cytotoxic T cell destroys a virus-infected body cell?
cards.back: 1) Its receptor binds a matching antigen on the infected cell. 2) Cytokines from helper T cells activate it, and it divides by clonal expansion. 3) It releases **perforin**, which forms pores in the infected cell membrane. 4) The infected cell dies.

cards.front: What does perforin do, and which cell releases it?
cards.back: **Perforin** is a protein released by cytotoxic T cells. It forms pores in the membrane of a target cell, so the cell dies.

cards.front: Why are antibodies unable to remove a virus that is hidden inside body cells?
cards.back: Antibodies act outside cells, in blood and tissue fluid, so they cannot reach the virus inside. **Cytotoxic T cells** can destroy the infected cell itself.

cards.front: Why are healthy cells near an infected cell usually left unharmed by a cytotoxic T cell?
cards.back: The cytotoxic T cell only kills cells that display the **matching antigen**. Healthy neighbouring cells do not display it, so they are not targeted.

cards.front: When comparing B cells and T cells, why is an answer that describes only B cells insufficient?
cards.back: You must state both cell types for each feature being compared. Writing only about B cells earns no comparison mark.

cards.front: What is an antigen-presenting cell and what does it do?
cards.back: An **antigen-presenting cell**, such as a macrophage, displays antigens from a digested pathogen on its surface membrane, which activates T cells.
cards.hint: Think about where the pathogen is broken down.

cards.front: How do B cells and T cells work together in a single infection?
cards.back: The **helper T cell** releases cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Memory cells of both types then give faster protection on a second exposure.
cards.hint: Think about what links B cells to cytotoxic T cells.
